narr: In this section, we'll explore the differences between present simple and present continuous tenses in business contexts.
We'll examine five exercises that help distinguish between general/permanent actions and current/temporary ones.

data.heading: Present Simple vs Present Continuous
bullets: Present Simple: general/permanent actions, routines, facts
Present Continuous: current/temporary actions, ongoing situations

narr: Let's start by understanding the core difference between these two tenses.
The present simple is used for things that are generally true, permanent, or habitual.
The present continuous, on the other hand, describes actions happening right now or temporary situations.

data.heading: Problem 1 — Routine vs Moment of Speaking
data.problem: Decide if the speaker is talking about routine activities or activities going on at the moment of speaking. Put the verbs into the present simple or the present continuous.

steps.text: Interviewer: Do you usually organize (you/usually organize) the delivery of milk to the factory? (the farmers/bring) it here themselves?
Bill: No, (we/always collect) the milk ourselves, and the tankers (deliver) it to the pasteurization plant twice a day.
Interviewer: What sort of quality control procedures (you/have)?
Bill: As a rule we (test) samples of every consignment, and then the milk (pass) down insulated pipes to the bottling plant, which (operate) 24 hours a day.
I'll show you round a bit later, but the production line (not work) at the moment because the employees (change) shifts.

data.result: Answers: (1) Do you usually organize (example); (2) Do the farmers bring (routine); (3) we always collect (routine; adverb before the main verb); (4) deliver (routine); (5) do you have (permanent state); (6) test (as a rule signals routine); (7) passes (general truth about the process); (8) operates (permanent); (9) isn't working (at the moment → present continuous); (10) are changing (happening now).

narr: Our first exercise comes from an interview with Bill Cogges in the dairy business.
Let's analyze each sentence to determine whether we should use present simple or present continuous.
The first question asks about Bill's usual activities - organizing deliveries.
This is clearly a routine, so we use present simple: 'Do you usually organize'.
The second question asks if farmers bring the milk themselves.
This is also a routine question, so we use present simple: 'Do the farmers bring'.
Bill responds that they always collect the milk themselves.
The adverb 'always' before the main verb indicates a routine, so present simple: 'we always collect'.
He then mentions that tankers deliver milk to the plant twice a day.
This is a scheduled routine, so present simple: 'deliver'.
The interviewer asks about quality control procedures.
This refers to a permanent state of the business, so present simple: 'do you have'.
Bill explains they test samples as a rule.
The phrase 'as a rule' signals a routine, so present simple: 'test'.
He then describes the general process of milk passing through pipes.
This is a general truth about the process, so present simple: 'passes'.
The bottling plant operates 24 hours a day.
This is a permanent characteristic, so present simple: 'operate'.
Finally, Bill notes the production line isn't working at the moment.
This is happening now, so present continuous: 'isn't working'.
The employees are changing shifts right now.
This is an ongoing action at the moment, so present continuous: 'are changing'.

data.heading: Problem 2 — General Activities vs Current Projects
data.problem: Complete the sentences with the correct form of the verbs in parentheses. Some refer to general activities, others to current projects.

steps.text: We set up the company in 2002 with a grant from the local government. We 1 (provide) IT backup and support for a number of small and medium-sized businesses in the area. We also 2 (design) web sites for local companies, and we 3 (look) after them by doing regular maintenance, and so on. When we 4 (get) a new customer, we always 5 (spend) a long time talking to them to find out their needs.

At the moment we 6 (set up) a website for a large local travel agency, and in fact our chief programmer is in charge of that project. She 7 (have) discussions with them to find out what sort of features they 8 (require).

data.result: Answers: (2) design (general activity); (3) look; (4) get (whenever-clause → present simple); (5) spend; (6) are setting up (at the moment); (7) is having (ongoing now); (8) require (stative verb → simple even now, Rule 4).

narr: In our second exercise, we look at general activities versus current projects.
The company provides IT backup and support for businesses.
This is a general activity they regularly do, so present simple: 'provide'.
They also design websites for local companies.
This is another general activity, so present simple: 'design'.
They look after these websites with regular maintenance.
This is part of their regular service, so present simple: 'look'.
When they get a new customer, they spend time talking to them.
The 'when' clause indicates a routine situation, so present simple: 'get' and 'spend'.
At the moment, they are setting up a website for a travel agency.
The phrase 'at the moment' indicates current activity, so present continuous: 'are setting up'.
Their chief programmer is having discussions with the client.
This is ongoing now, so present continuous: 'is having'.
The client requires certain features for their website.
Although this is happening now, 'require' is a stative verb that typically uses present simple even for current states, so present simple: 'require'.

data.heading: Problem 3 — Permanent vs Temporary Situations
data.problem: Complete the sentences with the correct form of the verbs in parentheses. Some describe permanent situations, others temporary ones.

steps.text: 1. He joined the company 25 years ago and he still works (work) for us. (example)
2. We (not/send) out any orders this week because we're waiting for the new lists.
3. I (deal) with Mr Matsumi's clients this week because he's away.
4. Go down this road, turn right, and the road (lead) straight to the industrial estate.
5. Because of the Euro/Dollar exchange rate, EU exports (not/do) very well at the moment.
6. The stock market is risky because the price of shares (vary) according to economic conditions.

narr: Our third exercise focuses on distinguishing between permanent and temporary situations.
The first sentence shows someone who has worked at the company for 25 years and still works there.
This is a permanent situation, so present simple: 'works'.
The second sentence mentions not sending orders this week.
The phrase 'this week' indicates a temporary situation, so present continuous: 'aren't sending'.
The third sentence talks about dealing with clients this week.
Again, 'this week' indicates a temporary situation, so present continuous: 'am dealing'.

data.heading: Problem 3 — Permanent vs Temporary Situations (cont.)

steps.text: 7. I (learn) French because I'm going to be based in the Paris office next year.
8. Hello. I'm Heinrich Brandt, I'm German, and I (come) from a small town near Munich.

data.result: Answers: (2) aren't sending (temporary — this week); (3) am dealing (temporary — this week); (4) leads (permanent fact about the road); (5) aren't doing (temporary — at the moment); (6) vary (permanent characteristic); (7) am learning (temporary, time-limited plan); (8) come (permanent fact about himself).

narr: The fourth sentence describes a road that leads to an industrial estate.
This is a permanent fact about the road, so present simple: 'leads'.
The fifth sentence discusses EU exports not doing well at the moment.
The phrase 'at the moment' indicates a temporary situation, so present continuous: 'aren't doing'.
The sixth sentence explains that stock prices vary with economic conditions.
This is a permanent characteristic of the market, so present simple: 'vary'.
The seventh sentence mentions learning French for a future position.
This is a temporary, time-limited plan, so present continuous: 'am learning'.
The eighth sentence introduces someone and states where he comes from.
This is a permanent fact about himself, so present simple: 'come'.

data.heading: Problem 4 — Facts vs Slow Changes
data.problem: In the following newspaper article, decide whether the verbs refer to general statements about change, or to changes that are currently taking place.

steps.text: Governments cannot last for ever. Normally political parties 1 (enjoy) a period of great popularity in their early years, then they 2 (go) through a period of stability and 3 (put) their ideas into practice. After that, they 4 (run) out of ideas, and the opposition 5 (take) power.

Now it 6 (seem) that the present government 7 (begin) to run into difficulties, and people 8 (start) to criticize the Prime Minister. The newspapers 9 (attack) other ministers because of the state of schools, public transport and hospitals, and the government 10 (lose) popularity.

data.result: Answers: (2) go; (3) put; (4) run; (5) takes (all general statements → present simple); (6) seems (stative verb, Rule 4); (7) is beginning; (8) are starting; (9) are attacking; (10) is losing (changes currently taking place → present continuous).

narr: Our fourth exercise examines the difference between facts and slow changes in a political context.
The first part describes the general lifecycle of political parties.
Political parties enjoy a period of popularity in their early years.
This is a general statement about how politics works, so present simple: 'enjoy'.
They then go through a period of stability.
This is another general statement, so present simple: 'go'.
They put their ideas into practice during this period.
Again, this is a general statement, so present simple: 'put'.
After that, they run out of ideas.
This is part of the general pattern, so present simple: 'run'.
The opposition takes power when this happens.
This is a general consequence, so present simple: 'takes'.
The second part shifts to current changes in the present government.
It seems that the present government is beginning to have difficulties.
'Seem' is a stative verb that typically uses present simple, so present simple: 'seem'.
The government is beginning to run into difficulties.
This describes a change currently taking place, so present continuous: 'is beginning'.
People are starting to criticize the Prime Minister.
This is a current change, so present continuous: 'are starting'.
The newspapers are attacking other ministers.
This describes current action, so present continuous: 'are attacking'.
The government is losing popularity.
This describes a change currently taking place, so present continuous: 'is losing'.

data.heading: Problem 5 — Stative Verbs
data.problem: In each of the following sentences, put one of the verbs into the present simple and the other into the present continuous.

steps.text: 1. We are interviewing (interview) people from outside the company for the new post in the export department, but I think (think) we ought to give the job to Mr Janousek. (example)
2. At the moment we (carry) out a survey to find out what sort of after-sales service our customers (want).
3. We've got a competition on at work to find a name for our new range of cosmetics. The marketing people (try) to find a brand name that (sound) natural and sophisticated.
4. (you/know) what Mrs Ericson (do)? She's not in her office and nobody has seen her since lunch.

data.result: Answers: (1) are interviewing, think (example); (2) are carrying, want; (3) are trying, sounds; (4) Do you know, is doing.

narr: Our final exercise focuses on stative verbs and how they interact with present continuous.
In the first example, they are interviewing people for a position.
This is an action happening now, so present continuous: 'are interviewing'.
However, the speaker thinks they should give the job to Mr Janousek.
'Think' as an opinion is a stative verb that typically uses present simple, so present simple: 'think'.
In the second sentence, they are carrying out a survey at the moment.
This is current action, so present continuous: 'are carrying'.
They want to know about after-sales service.
'Want' as a state of mind is typically present simple, even when referring to current needs, so present simple: 'want'.
In the third sentence, marketing people are trying to find a brand name.
This is current effort, so present continuous: 'are trying'.
They want a name that sounds natural and sophisticated.
'Sound' as a sensory perception is a stative verb that typically uses present simple, so present simple: 'sounds'.
In the final sentence, you are asked if you know what Mrs Ericson does.
'Know' is a stative verb indicating state of knowledge, so present simple: 'Do you know'.
The question is about what she is doing right now.
This is current action, so present continuous: 'is doing'.

data.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Present simple: general truths, permanent situations, routines
Present continuous: current actions, temporary situations
Some verbs (stative verbs) typically use present simple even for current states
Time expressions help determine which tense to use

narr: Let's summarize what we've learned about present simple and present continuous in business contexts.
Remember that present simple is used for general truths, permanent situations, and routines.
Present continuous, on the other hand, is used for current actions and temporary situations.
Some verbs, known as stative verbs, typically use present simple even when referring to current states.
Time expressions like 'usually', 'always', 'at the moment', and 'this week' can help determine which tense to use.
